title: Dead Wrong, in Front of Congress
author: Ray Dalio
wiifm: The week ends with the hardest problem: how to build an organisation that keeps making good decisions when the founder is wrong. Ray Dalio found out the hard way, losing nearly everything after a confident public prediction in 1982. What he built afterwards, Bridgewater Associates, became the largest hedge fund in the world and one of the strangest workplaces anywhere. You will follow him from a caddie's bag on Long Island to a one-man firm and back, and leave with tools for learning from mistakes, deciding whose judgement to trust, and a sharp warning about what happens when nobody can overrule the boss.

b: Raymond Thomas Dalio was born on the eighth of August 1949 in Jackson Heights, Queens, in New York City. His father, Marino, was a jazz musician who played clarinet and saxophone in Manhattan clubs. His mother, Ann, was a homemaker. When Ray was eight the family moved out to Manhasset, a comfortable suburb on Long Island.

He was, by his own account, a poor and bored student who did not like being told what to memorise. What he liked was money and independence. He had a paper round, shovelled snow, mowed lawns, and at about twelve became a caddie at the Links Golf Club, a private course whose members included serious figures from Wall Street. Carrying their bags, he listened to them talk about the stock market.

At twelve he made his first investment: about three hundred dollars, by his own memory, in Northeast Airlines, chosen because it was the only company he had heard of trading for under five dollars a share. Soon afterwards another airline agreed to merge with it, and the shares roughly tripled. He was hooked.

He later admitted he had simply been lucky. But the experience planted the habit that would define him. He started to read company reports and look for patterns, and he was soon convinced that he could see where markets were going. That confidence would make him, and very nearly ruin him.
ch.cap: Caddie Ray, twelve, overhears Wall Street men talking stocks

b: Dalio studied finance at Long Island University's C. W. Post campus, where he did far better than at school because he cared about the subject, and he also took up Transcendental Meditation in 1968, a habit he kept for life. In the summer of 1971 he was working as a clerk on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange.

On the evening of the fifteenth of August 1971, President Richard Nixon went on television and announced that the United States would no longer convert dollars into gold. Dalio assumed this was a disaster and that the stock market would crash. Instead, the next day it rose sharply. He had been confidently wrong.

Rather than shrug, he went to work out why. He discovered that the same thing had happened in 1933, when President Franklin Roosevelt had cut the link between the dollar and gold. Printing money and devaluing the currency had pushed up the prices of shares and other assets. Events that looked unique, he realised, often repeat in patterns, and the patterns can be studied.

That became his method for life. Look for the historical cases that resemble the present, understand the cause and effect behind them, and write rules from them. He went on to Harvard Business School, graduating in 1973, then traded commodities and worked as a broker. He was fired from one job, partly for punching his boss on New Year's Eve, he later said.
ch.cap: After Nixon cuts gold, stocks soar instead of crashing

b: In 1975, aged twenty-six, Dalio founded Bridgewater Associates from his two-bedroom apartment in Manhattan. At first it was a small consultancy, advising companies on how to manage the risk of swinging prices in currencies, interest rates and commodities.

One problem shows how he thought. In the early 1980s McDonald's wanted to launch a chicken product but could not make the numbers work. Chicken prices moved around too much, and a fixed menu price can be wiped out by volatile costs. McDonald's asked its supplier to agree a fixed price. The supplier refused, because his own costs were unpredictable.

Dalio's insight was that a chicken, in economic terms, is mostly corn and soybean meal, since that is what it costs to feed one. You could not hedge chickens, but you could hedge corn and soybean meal on the futures markets. So he helped design a hedge on the feed, which let the supplier lock in his costs and offer McDonald's a fixed price. The Chicken McNugget went on sale across America in 1983.

Dalio tells the story himself, and it is a lovely example of breaking a problem into its real inputs and controlling the ones you can. But be careful about how much credit to give. The McNugget had many parents, from food scientists to suppliers, and the hedge was one piece of a much larger effort.
ch.cap: A chicken is really corn and soybean meal, hedged

b: By 1982 Dalio was convinced that America had borrowed too much and that a debt crisis was coming. In August that year Mexico defaulted on its debts, just as he had warned. He became briefly famous. He testified before Congress in November and appeared on television, on Louis Rukeyser's programme Wall Street Week, saying with complete confidence that there would be no soft landing, and that a depression might follow.

Then the Federal Reserve cut interest rates, and instead of collapsing, the American stock market began one of the greatest bull runs in its history. Dalio had bet heavily the other way. He lost money for his clients and for himself. He had to let go every member of staff, people he thought of almost as family, until Bridgewater was a firm of one person. To pay his household bills he borrowed four thousand dollars from his father.
His later summary is three words: I was dead wrong. He also says it was one of the best things that ever happened to him.

That is the hinge of the whole book. In the wreckage he asked himself one question. How do you get the benefits of having strong opinions without being destroyed when they are wrong? Everything in Principles is the answer. His conclusion was not to stop having strong views. It was to build a way of testing them, and to surround himself with people who would challenge him.
ch.cap: Bridgewater shrinks to one man while the market soars

b: The most famous line Dalio ever wrote is a formula: pain plus reflection equals progress. It is not a motivational slogan. It is a claim about where useful information is found. Painful results contain the best evidence of the gap between how you think the world works and how it actually works. But only if you reflect, and most people do not. The natural response to pain is to blame bad luck, explain it away, or move on.

His way of forcing reflection was simple. Before each trade he wrote down his reasoning and the criteria behind the decision. When the result arrived, he could compare it with what he had actually thought, rather than with a flattering memory of it. Over the years the criteria became rules, the rules became a list, the list circulated inside Bridgewater, then went online as a free document downloaded millions of times, and in 2017 became this book.
That history matters. Principles is not a theory that was later applied. It is the residue of thousands of specific corrections.

He also names two barriers to learning, and they need different cures. The ego barrier is the emotional need to be right, which makes disagreement feel like an attack, so people argue to win rather than to find out. The cure is to treat disagreement as information you were missing. The blind spot barrier is worse, because effort cannot fix it. Everyone's mind has a shape: some people see detail and miss the big picture, some see possibilities and miss risks. You cannot see what you are not built to see. The only cure is other people with different blind spots, arranged so that they will actually speak up. Dalio calls the habit of welcoming them radical open-mindedness.
ch.cap: Dalio writes down his reasoning before every trade

b: As Bridgewater rebuilt and grew, Dalio faced a problem every organisation has. If the boss decides everything, the firm is limited by his blind spots. If decisions are made by vote, the views of people with great track records are averaged with the views of people with none, and the result is mush.

His answer was believability-weighted decision making. Everyone's opinion counts, but not equally. To be believable on a question, a person must meet two tests. They must have succeeded at that specific thing at least three times. And they must be able to explain the cause and effect behind how they did it. A track record without an explanation may be luck. An explanation without a track record may be theory. And believability belongs to a subject: being an expert on bonds says nothing about your judgement on hiring.

Bridgewater built software for this. With a tool called the Dot Collector, people rated each other in meetings, live, on dozens of qualities. Over time each person built up a profile of strengths and weaknesses that Dalio compared to a baseball card, visible to colleagues. When people disagreed, the system could show the believability-weighted view as well as the simple majority.

His operating loop was a five-step process. Set clear goals. Identify the problems in the way and do not tolerate them. Diagnose their root causes. Design a plan. Then do it. The commonest failure is jumping from spotting a problem straight to a solution, skipping diagnosis, so the fix treats a symptom while the cause keeps producing new ones. He also noted that the five steps need different temperaments and almost nobody is good at all of them, so you should know which you are bad at and find people who are good at them.
ch.cap: Colleagues rate each other live with the Dot Collector

b: Bridgewater's most notorious feature was radical transparency. Nearly every meeting was recorded, and the recordings were available to staff. The idea was coherent. If people can see how decisions are really made, they learn faster, nobody can misrepresent anyone, and office politics becomes hard because there is no private version of events.

The emblematic story is an email Dalio received after a client meeting from an employee named Jim Haskel. It told him plainly that he deserved a D-minus for his performance: he had rambled, and he had not prepared. Dalio did not punish him. He shared the email around the company, and later showed it on screen during a TED talk in 2017. The message was meant to be clear. The culture applies to the founder too.
He was honest that many people cannot bear it. By his own account a large share of new hires left within about eighteen months, and he treated that as the culture filtering properly.

The other big idea is that an organisation is a machine made of people and culture. The manager's job is to stand above it, looking down, and compare what it produces with what it was designed to produce. When there is a gap, the fault is either in the design or in a part, and both can be fixed without blame. From this comes his hiring rule: values first, then abilities, then skills, because skills are easiest to learn and values almost impossible to change. And from it comes the hard truth that keeping someone in a role they cannot do is not kindness.
ch.cap: The founder's D-minus email goes up on the big screen

ch.h: An autocracy with an audit trail?
b: The results were spectacular. Bridgewater became the largest hedge fund in the world, managing around a hundred and sixty billion dollars at its peak in 2019. Its main fund, Pure Alpha, launched in 1991, earned strong long-run returns and famously made money for clients in 2008, when almost everyone else was losing. It also had a flat stretch through much of the 2010s and lost money in 2020.

The serious criticism came in 2023 with The Fund, a book by the journalist Rob Copeland. His central allegation was not that the culture was harsh, which Bridgewater never hid. It was that the system worked almost in reverse of how it was advertised. On his account, investment decisions depended far more on Dalio's personal judgement than on any weighted system, and the ratings and recordings worked less as a meritocracy than as a tool of control, in which the founder's own believability could never really be marked down. Dalio and Bridgewater strongly disputed the book.

You do not need to settle who is right to see the structural lesson. Any system that weights opinions by believability must answer one hard question: who sets the scores, and can the person at the top ever be scored down? If not, it is not a meritocracy of ideas. It is an autocracy with an audit trail, and the audit trail makes it more persuasive, not less. In a small firm the danger is automatic, because the owner's score is set by the fact that they own the place.
Dalio handed over control gradually, a process he admitted was difficult, and he gave up his last formal control of the firm in 2022.
ch.cap: The founder's chair sits above the ratings and recordings

b: Look back across this week and the five lives connect. Adam Smith described how wealth is created by specialisation and trade. Peter Thiel showed that competition competes the profit away, so you need something rivals cannot copy. Rockefeller showed what that looks like in practice, glory and crime together. Munger taught the discipline of not losing it. And Dalio faced the last problem: how to build something that thinks better than the person who started it.

His own answer has flaws, and the best of Principles survives them. Write your reasoning down before you know the outcome, so hindsight cannot flatter you. Keep diagnosis separate from solution, and do not leave diagnosis until the root cause is named, even when the cause is a person in the wrong role. Know which of the five steps you are personally bad at, and get help there.

Decide in advance whose judgement counts on which kind of question, based on real track records rather than job titles, and make sure the answer is not always you. In a small firm, the owner speaking first usually ends the discussion, so on questions where someone else has the record, speak last or not at all.

And treat the people who tell you unwelcome things as the scarcest resource in the business. In a firm you own, they genuinely are. Dalio learned that by losing everything in 1982. The point of reading his life is that you do not have to.
ch.cap: Monday's desk holds a pin, knight, barrel, sweets, notebook

take: For each significant decision, write what you expect, the two or three assumptions behind it, and a review date. Within a year your mistakes will cluster into patterns, and those are your real principles.
When something goes badly, resist the urge to blame luck and move on. Spend fifteen minutes writing what the result reveals about the gap between your model and reality.
Do not jump from a problem to a solution. Stay with the question of root cause until you can name it, even if it is uncomfortable, such as the wrong person in a role.
For each recurring decision, such as pricing, hiring or complaints, write down whose judgement carries most weight and why, based on track record rather than title.
In a small firm the owner's opinion offered first ends the discussion. On questions where someone else has more experience, ask for their view before giving yours.
Goals, problem spotting, diagnosis, design and execution need different strengths. Be honest about which you are poor at and staff around them.
Skills can be taught and values rarely change. Write down what the role needs before meeting candidates so you do not rationalise towards whoever you liked.
Make sure you can be overruled
Any system for weighing opinions fails if the person at the top can never be marked down. Build in a real way for someone to tell you that you are wrong, and reward them when they do.
recall: What did Dalio get wrong in 1982, and what did it cost him?

After correctly predicting Mexico's default, he declared publicly, including to Congress, that a depression would follow with no soft landing. The Federal Reserve eased and a great bull market began; he lost his clients' money and his own, let go all his staff and borrowed four thousand dollars from his father.
What lesson did he take from Nixon's decision in August 1971?

He expected the end of the dollar's link to gold to crash the stock market, but it rose. Studying why, he found the same thing had happened in 1933, and concluded that events repeat in patterns that can be studied and turned into rules.
What are the two barriers to learning, and how do their cures differ?

The ego barrier, the emotional need to be right, is cured by treating disagreement as useful information. The blind spot barrier, the inability to see what your mind is not built to see, can only be cured by other people with different blind spots who are willing to speak up.
What two tests make someone believable on a question?
They must have succeeded at that specific thing at least three times, and be able to explain the cause and effect behind how they did it. Believability applies only to that subject.
What is the central structural criticism of believability weighting?

Someone must set the scores, and if the person at the top can never be scored down, the system becomes an autocracy with an audit trail. In a small firm this happens automatically unless it is deliberately designed against.
note: Biographical details come from Dalio's own account in Principles, including Northeast Airlines, the 1971 lesson, the 1982 testimony and the four thousand dollar loan. His role in the Chicken McNugget is his own telling and should be seen as one contribution among many. Bridgewater asset figures are widely reported. Rob Copeland's The Fund of 2023 makes the main critical allegations, which Dalio and Bridgewater dispute; Pure Alpha is usually dated to 1991.
words: Excessive pride or self-confidence that invites a fall.

To protect against a loss by taking an offsetting position, often in futures markets.

A system in which influence and reward go to those with proven ability rather than rank or connections.
Bridgewater's believability weighting was meant to be a meritocracy of ideas, where people with real track records on a question carry more weight.
Rule by one person whose authority cannot effectively be challenged.

stories: Ray Dalio grew up on Long Island, a jazz musician's son and a bored, poor student. At about twelve he became a caddie at a private golf club whose members included serious Wall Street figures, and carrying their bags he heard them talk about shares. So he bought some: about three hundred dollars' worth, by his own memory, of Northeast Airlines, chosen for one reason only. But he was hooked, and convinced he could see where markets were going.

In 1982 Ray Dalio had called the Mexican debt default correctly, and he was briefly famous. He testified before Congress and told a national television audience, with complete confidence, that there would be no soft landing, and that a depression might follow. Then the Federal Reserve cut interest rates, and the American stock market began one of the greatest rises in its history. Dalio had bet the other way. He lost his clients' money and his own, let every member of staff go until Bridgewater was a firm of one, and borrowed four thousand dollars from his father to pay the household bills. He calls it one of the best things that ever happened to him.
A D minus for the boss

After a client meeting, Ray Dalio, founder of the largest hedge fund in the world, received an email from an employee named Jim Haskel. It told him plainly that his performance deserved a D minus. He had rambled, and he had not prepared. In most firms that email would have ended a career. Dalio did not punish Haskel. He shared the message around the company, and years later put it on screen during a TED talk in 2017. The point was meant to be unmistakable: the rules apply to the founder too. Whether they really did is exactly what his critics later disputed.
biz: Log your predictions before the results

Dalio wrote down his reasoning before each trade so hindsight could not flatter him. Start a simple decision log this week. Before any campaign proposal, new lender panel, script change or hire, write what you expect to happen, the two or three assumptions behind it, and a review date. For ad changes proposed to whoever runs the accounts, record the expected cost per completed loan in advance. Review monthly. Add a Consumer Duty column: what you expect to happen to complaints, customer understanding and outcomes. Within months the misses will cluster, and those patterns are your real principles.
Make sure the owner can be overruled

Copeland's warning is that a system can look like a meritocracy while the founder can never be marked down. In a small FCA firm that is a real risk. Write down who has the final say on recurring calls: lender choice, vulnerable customer handling, complaints and financial promotions, based on track record and competence, not ownership. Give your compliance lead, or an external compliance adviser, an explicit right to stop something you want, and record when they do. On questions where an adviser knows more, ask for their view first and speak last.
connects: Dalio's habit of writing his reasoning down before the outcome and scoring it afterwards is the core discipline Tetlock found in the best forecasters.
Dalio's five step loop of goals, problems, diagnosis, design and doing is a learning cycle much like Boyd's loop of observing, orienting, deciding and acting faster than reality punishes you.
Dalio's systems for exposing blind spots share Munger's aim of being consistently not stupid by inverting, checking and inviting disagreement rather than trusting raw brilliance.
recap:
Ray Dalio was a jazz musician's son from Queens who did badly at school and well at making money. At twelve, caddying for Wall Street men on Long Island, he bought shares in Northeast Airlines simply because they were cheap. A merger tripled them. He later admitted it was luck, but he was hooked, and convinced he could see where markets were going.

In nineteen seventy-one, when President Nixon cut the dollar's link to gold, Dalio expected a crash. The market rose. Instead of shrugging, he dug into history and found the same thing had happened in nineteen thirty-three. That became his method: find past cases that resemble the present, understand the cause and effect, and write rules.

In nineteen seventy-five he started Bridgewater from his flat in Manhattan. Then came the fall. In nineteen eighty-two he told Congress and a television audience, with total confidence, that there would be no soft landing. The market began one of its greatest ever rises. He lost his clients' money and his own, let every employee go, and borrowed four thousand dollars from his father to pay the bills. His verdict was three words: dead wrong.

That failure produced the first big idea. Pain plus reflection equals progress. Painful results reveal the gap between how you think the world works and how it really works, but only if you stop and study them. So write your reasoning down before the result arrives, and hindsight cannot flatter you.

The second idea is that your own mind is the obstacle. Ego makes you argue to win, and blind spots hide what you are not built to see. The cure is people who think differently and who will actually speak up.

The third is believability. Count everyone's view, but weight it by a real track record on that particular question, together with a clear explanation of how they succeeded.

The fourth is a loop of five steps: goals, problems, diagnosis, design and doing, with the warning never to skip diagnosis and jump straight to a fix.

Bridgewater became the largest hedge fund in the world, with recorded meetings and live ratings of colleagues. An employee once emailed Dalio that he deserved a D minus for a meeting, and Dalio shared it with the whole firm. Yet a twenty twenty-three book by the journalist Rob Copeland alleged that the system mostly served its founder, a charge Dalio disputes.

That leaves the fifth idea, and the hardest. Any system for weighing judgement fails if the person at the top can never be marked down. Build one where you can be told you are wrong, and remember his formula: pain plus reflection equals progress.
